strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision question: whether multilingual captions contribute visual information beyond additional captions in one language. Its empirical contribution could inform dataset construction and caption evaluation without requiring a new architecture or benchmark record.

The comparisons use the same images and matched caption counts, with consistent annotation instructions in Crossmodal. Table 1 reports substantial differences, including 4.35 objects for multilingual sets versus 2.98 averaged across monolingual sets. Similar trends across human captions, LLaVA, and Vertex provide worthwhile supporting evidence.

The Visual Genome experiment strengthens the evidence beyond unconstrained graph size: Table 3 shows Vertex object coverage increasing from 9.6% for English captions to 11.7% for English–French–Chinese captions. The supplementary English/Japanese user study and native-speaker translation evaluation are additional, relevant validation efforts.
weaknesses: The fine-tuning evidence contains a consequential reporting inconsistency. All 36 entries in Table 14, attributed to LLaVA captions, exactly match the corresponding entries in Table 4, attributed to Vertex captions, despite supposedly different training and evaluation data. This leaves the claimed replication across caption sources unverified. Table 10 also identifies multilingual training as best on the multilingual evaluation set, whereas Tables 4 and 15 give higher scores to French-trained models: 0.246 versus 0.244 and 0.154 versus 0.151, respectively.

The central graph-size measurements need stronger validation as measures of additional visual information. Parsing and canonicalization can count alternative descriptions of the same content as new concepts. In Figure 2, the multilingual graph adds a 'word' object for the revolution inscription, although the English captions already describe that inscription. No quantitative parser audit or canonicalization sensitivity analysis establishes how often this occurs. The Visual Genome check supports increased object recall, but does not establish the precision of additional concepts or validate the reported relation and attribute gains.

The expressive-variation claims are less securely supported than the object-coverage findings. The translation audit assesses factual preservation, not preservation of tone, authenticity, or other LIWC dimensions; Appendix 8.1 also samples generated captions rather than the human Crossmodal captions underlying the headline results. LIWC scores are not validated for this setting of short, translated captions. Near-chance language classification with one embedding-based linear classifier cannot establish that translation artifacts are absent.

Several interpretations exceed what the experiments identify. Section 3.2 cannot rule out language-conditioned generation modes merely because multilingual and multiple-model caption sets have similar graph sizes; there is no justified prediction separating those explanations. Likewise, language-matched reference performance demonstrates distribution adaptation, but does not establish improved visual representations. Caption length and information density are not controlled, limiting attribution of larger unions specifically to complementary concept selection.

Reproducibility is limited by missing model checkpoint identifiers, generation settings, graph-merging thresholds, and fine-tuning hyperparameters. The primary comparisons lack uncertainty estimates and clearly specified statistical procedures, although selected supplementary comparisons report significance. Separately, correctable reporting errors include attributing the 46.0%/66.1%/66.8% gains to an English-specific comparison when they correspond to multilingual versus monolingual averages, and reporting a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98 despite every constituent value being at most 1.86. These arithmetic issues alone would not determine rejection; the decisive concerns are measurement validity and the unresolved reliability of the fine-tuning evidence.
